proof:
# An all-dimensional mass-dependent centroid inequality

Let d>=1 and Gamma_d=(d/(d+1))^d. Let K be a d-dimensional convex
body and let eta be a finite measure satisfying 0<=eta<=1_K dx.
Let g be the centroid of rho=1_K dx+2eta. Then every closed halfspace
H containing g satisfies the strict inequality

    |K intersect H|+eta(H)
       >(3/4)Gamma_d (|K|+eta(K)).                       (1)

This is an ordinary continuous auxiliary theorem, with a complete
dimension-uniform proof below. The subsequent application uses an
independently proved dominated midpoint coupling of two equal-volume
convex bodies. It does not assert full OC in arbitrary integer dimension.

## 1. Actual centroid, cap quantiles, and the scalar constraint

Normalize |K|=1 and set alpha=eta(K), so 0<=alpha<=1. The actual
centroid g is interior to K, since the rho density is at least one
throughout K and every supporting linear functional has strictly
smaller average than its maximum. It suffices to move the halfspace
boundary inward to g. Put s=|K intersect H| in(0,1) and r=eta(H).

For its scalar projection X, let V(t)=|K intersect{X>=t}| and
G(t)=V(t)^(1/d). The inclusion of Minkowski combinations of caps in
intermediate caps and Brunn--Minkowski show that G is concave. The
projection distribution has a continuous strictly increasing cumulative
law on its support interval, so V(X) is uniform on[0,1] under volume.
The pushforward of eta has a density h(v) between zero and one. It has
mass alpha and mass r on[0,s]. Jensen at the centroid gives

    (1+2alpha)s^(1/d)
       >=d/(d+1)+2 integral_0^1 v^(1/d)h(v)dv.

For an increasing function, a density bounded above by one and with
prescribed mass on an interval minimizes its integral when placed at
the left end. To prove this directly, subtract that left-interval
indicator and then subtract the integrand's value at the cutoff; the
resulting integrand is nonnegative on both sides. Applying this on
[0,s] and[s,1], with q=1+1/d, gives

    q(1+2alpha)s^(q-1)
       >=1+2r^q+2(s+alpha-r)^q-2s^q.                    (2)

All intervals fit by domination: 0<=r<=s and alpha-r<=1-s. Define

    U=1/s, E=r/s, Q=(s+alpha-r)/s,
    phi(t)=t-[d/(d+1)]t^(1+1/d), t>=0.

Dividing(2) by q s^q and using alpha=s(Q+E-1) gives exactly

    phi(U)+2phi(Q)+2phi(E)>=2/(d+1).                    (3)

Every measure used here is absolutely continuous; closed boundaries
carry zero relevant volume. These arguments also apply when d=1,
where the projection law is simply uniform on an interval.

## 2. The mass-dependent dual objective

Write A=1/Gamma_d=(1+1/d)^d and set

    L=4A/3-1, D=U+Q-L E.

The desired normalized assertion s+r>(3/(4A))(1+alpha) is equivalent
to

    D<1+4A/3,                                         (4)

because (1+alpha)/s=U+Q+E-1. Elementary one-variable maximization
gives, for every real a and t>=0,

    phi(t)+a t <= (1/(d+1))(1+a)_+^(d+1).              (5)

When a>-1 the maximizer is t=(1+a)^d; otherwise it is zero. Apply(5)
to U with a=1/d, to each of the two Q terms with a=1/(2d), and to
each of the two E terms with a=-L/(2d). Combining with(3) yields

    D <= [d/(d+1)] [ (1+1/d)^(d+1)
             +2(1+1/(2d))^(d+1)
             +2(1-L/(2d))_+^(d+1)-2 ].                (6)

Since (1+1/d)^(d+1)=(1+1/d)A, it is enough to prove

    Delta_d:=2+(1+1/d)(1+A/3)
       -2(1+1/(2d))^(d+1)
       -2(1-L/(2d))_+^(d+1)>0.                        (7)

The next two sections prove(7) for every integer d>=1 without an
asymptotic error or unspecified constant. Thus(4), and hence(1), follow.

## 3. All d>=14 by elementary inequalities

The function x log(1+1/x) is strictly increasing for x>0: its derivative
is log(1+1/x)-1/(x+1)>0, since
log(1+t)=integral_0^t(1+u)^(-1)du>t/(1+t) for t>0.
Thus A_d increases with d. The exact integer comparison

    8*15^14 > 21*14^14

gives A_d>=A_14>21/8 for d>=14, and hence L>5/2.

We use two elementary numerical bounds, with rational certificates.
The exponential series gives

    e<=8/3+(1/24)sum_(j>=0)5^(-j)=87/32<(33/20)^2,

because each successive factorial ratio after 1/4! is at most1/5.
Also its first seven positive terms give

    exp(5/4)>sum_(j=0)^6 (5/4)^j/j!
       =2058029/589824>80/23.

Therefore sqrt(e)<33/20 and exp(-5/4)<23/80. Using
(1+t)^m<exp(mt) and (1-t)_+^m<=exp(-mt),

    2(1+1/(2d))^(d+1)
       <2sqrt(e)(1+1/(2d))
       <33/10+33/(20d),
    2(1-L/(2d))_+^(d+1)<23/40.

Their sum is less than 31/8+33/(20d). In contrast the positive term
in(7) is at least 31/8+15/(8d). Since 15/8>33/20, (7) follows
strictly for every d>=14.

## 4. Explicit finite integer certificates for d=1,...,13

Here no exponential bound is needed. Define positive integers

    J=6d^(d+1),
    B=3(2d+1)d^d,
    N=3(2d+1)d^d-4(d+1)^d,
    Z=6d^(d+1)+3(d+1)d^d+(d+1)^(d+1).

For each of these thirteen dimensions N>0. Direct substitution in(7)
gives the exact identity

    Delta_d=2[Z J^d-B^(d+1)-N^(d+1)]/J^(d+1).           (8)

The positive integers R_d displayed in Appendix A are exactly

    R_d=16[Z J^d-B^(d+1)-N^(d+1)]-J^(d+1).

Consequently Delta_d=1/8+R_d/[8J^(d+1)]>1/8>0. Appendix A is an
explicit finite integer certificate, not decimal or numerical evidence.

The strictness is uniform over all halfspaces, which will matter when
taking a depth infimum. Set epsilon_d=d Delta_d/(d+1)>0. Equation(6)
in fact gives D<=1+4A/3-epsilon_d. Recovering the original masses,

    s+r>=(3/(4A))(1+alpha+epsilon_d s).

The initial centroid Jensen inequality alone gives
s>=Gamma_d/(1+2alpha)^d>=Gamma_d/3^d. Consequently(1) has the
dimension-only uniform positive surplus

    |K intersect H|+eta(H)
      >=(3/4)Gamma_d (|K|+eta(K))
          +[3 Gamma_d^2 epsilon_d/(4*3^d)] |K|.         (8a)

This proves strictness of the subsequent depth infimum; it is not
inferred merely from strictness for each individual cap.

## 5. The equal-endpoint mixed application

The proved dominated midpoint coupling theorem is supplied with a
direct conditional-Fubini proof in
`accepted fact 486fe778f838d99d, f6641f09c19819a3`;
the earlier proof is `candidate 71bcdfc8eb8340c6`.
Its exact statement used here is this: if A,B are d-dimensional convex
bodies of the same volume v, there is a coupling pi of their ordinary
volume measures, of total mass v, whose midpoint pushforward eta has
density at most one on M=(A+B)/2. Its first moment is
v(g_A+g_B)/2. Moreover, if the two endpoint halfspaces have normals u
and thresholds b+beta and b-beta, then

    eta{u.x>=b}
       <=|A intersect{u.x>=b+beta}|
          +|B intersect{u.x>=b-beta}|.                (9)

Indeed any pair whose midpoint is in that closed halfspace has at
least one endpoint in the corresponding closed endpoint halfspace.
The theorem constructs one actual coupling; no optimizing law or
unproved centroid prescription is assumed.

Let K contain M, and put A,K,B at integer bases -1,0,1. They are the
exact fibers of their convex hull. The true mixed centroid is

    Y=(0,g),
    g=[v g_A+|K|g_K+v g_B]/(|K|+2v).

It is the centroid of 1_K dx+2eta, and belongs to K since eta is
supported in K. For every nonvertical ambient halfspace through Y,
(9) and(1) therefore give

    D_S(Y)>(3/4)Gamma_d (|K|+v).                       (10)

A pure integer halfspace through Y contains K and one full endpoint;
its mass |K|+v strictly exceeds the right side of(10). Parallel inward
translation treats every containing halfspace. Thus(10) holds for all
closed ambient halfspaces at one deterministic actual point.
More precisely, all nonvertical caps have the uniform surplus(8a),
and the two pure integer orientations have gap
[1-(3/4)Gamma_d](|K|+v)>0. Taking the smaller of these two positive
numbers justifies the strict infimum in(10).

In particular(10) proves the full equal-endpoint edge target for
1<=|K|/v<=3, in every continuous dimension, with no restriction on
the endpoint shapes or on the containing middle shape. In fact the
displayed bound holds for every possible |K|>=v. This is a specific
three-fiber theorem; no decomposition of an arbitrary mixed-integer
body into such triples with preserved global mass has been asserted.
